scenario.name: Ledger Connect-Kit NPM Compromise & Web3 WalletConnect Drainer
scenario.overview: Picture an international border crossing checkpoint with glass passport inspection booths, zig-zag queue stanchions, an X-ray luggage conveyor belt, and a striped crossing barrier. Approaching the international border crossing, a traveler steps up to the glass passport booth carrying a travel booklet with a subtly altered entry stamp. In this real-world scenario, the intruder approaches the luggage x-ray belt & barrier disguised as a regular visitor, then moves quietly past the luggage x-ray belt & barrier into neighboring restricted rooms. A secondary customs officer cross-checks the border passport registry and catches a stamp serial number that was never issued by that embassy. In this scenario (T1195.001, Ledger Connect-Kit NPM Compromise & Web3 WalletConnect Drainer), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: former Employee NPM Token Phishing, then unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation, then rogue WalletConnect Modal. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Former Employee NPM Token Phishing, then Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation, then Rogue WalletConnect Modal, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Former Employee NPM Token Phishing & Publish of v1.1.5–1.1.7
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1195.001 - Compromise Software Dependencies)
stages.description: Approaching the international border crossing, a traveler steps up to the glass passport booth carrying a travel booklet with a subtly altered entry stamp. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder approaches the luggage x-ray belt & barrier disguised as a regular visitor while everyday visitors and the border customs officer go about their routine. After spear-phishing a former employee whose npmjs account had not been removed from the @ledgerhq organization during offboarding, the attacker generated an npm access token and published @ledgerhq/connect-kit versions 1.1.5, 1.1.6, and 1.1.7 directly from the CLI (bypassing the official GitHub repository and CI/CD release pipeline entirely). Auditing the npm registry metadata against GitHub showed that versions 1.1.5–1.1.7 had no corresponding Git tags, pull requests, or GitHub Actions release runs in Ledger’s source repository. In the documented Auth exchange from Angel Drainer Operator & Rogue ProjectID to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK T1195.001 (confirming that the Stage 1: Former Employee NPM Token Phishing & Publish of v1.1.5–1.1.7 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Former Employee NPM Token Phishing & Publish of v1.1.5–1.1.7 / ⇠#1 ACK T1195.001) from Node ① (#1 Angel Drainer Operator & Rogue ProjectID) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 User Web3 Wallet (Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll)).

stages.title: Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1059.007 - JavaScript)
stages.description: While the customs scanner checks only the outer cover of the passport, the forged interior page clears the glass booth and the striped crossing barrier swings upward. Here in Step 2 inside the border control, the intruder moves quietly past the luggage x-ray belt & barrier into neighboring restricted rooms without disturbing the diplomatic sealed pouch lane. Even dApps that pinned their own package-lock.json were impacted because @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader was designed to dynamically load <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@ledgerhq/connect-kit@1/dist/umd/index.min.js"> at runtime in the user’s browser (using the floating major version tag @1, which caused jsDelivr’s CDN to automatically resolve and serve the newly published 1.1.7 bundle within minutes). This design bypassed build-time dependency pinning completely: every time a user loaded a dApp frontend in their browser, the browser fetched the latest 1.x build directly from cdn.jsdelivr.net. In the documented WAF exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit), NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit) responds with ALERT T1059.007 (confirming that the Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader request succeeded on NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader / ⇠#2 ALERT T1059.007) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 User Web3 Wallet (Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll)).

keySpecs.value: Never dynamically load unpinned major-version scripts (`@1`) from public CDNs at runtime; bundle dependencies at build time with locked SHA-512 integrity hashes in package-lock.json.

stages.title: Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1657 - Financial Theft)
stages.description: Rolling luggage smoothly off the X-ray conveyor into the secure arrival hall, the traveler crosses the border wearing an official-looking entry clearance. In this final step inside the border control, the intruder moves quietly past the luggage x-ray belt & barrier into neighboring restricted rooms until the customs passport registry catches the mismatch. The injected Angel Drainer payload rendered a fake WalletConnect connection modal using an attacker-controlled WalletConnect Project ID, scanned the connected wallet’s token balances, and prompted the user to sign EIP-712 Permit2 off-chain messages or setApprovalForAll transactions (cryptographic token allowances that grant the attacker’s drainer smart contract permission to transfer the user’s ERC-20 tokens and NFTs without further confirmation). Ledger hardware wallets themselves remained secure, but users who blindly approved the malicious transaction prompt on their wallet screen authorized the transfer; Ledger and WalletConnect contained the incident within hours by revoking the rogue WalletConnect Project ID, purging jsDelivr’s cache, and shipping pinned v1.1.8. In the documented WAF exchange from NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit) to Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend, Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend responds with ALERT T1657 (confirming that the Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain request succeeded on Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend and completing the final execution objective of Ledger Connect-Kit NPM Compromise & Web3 WalletConnect Drainer). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain / ⇠#3 ALERT T1657) from Node ③ (#3 NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit)) to Node ④ (#4 Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 User Web3 Wallet (Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll)).
